title: Towards a Theoretical Foundation of Process Science
text:
Like numerous other terms in computing disciplines, the term “business process management” (BPM) is used to denote (a) a particular kind of problem, (b) a possible solution to that problem, and (c) the academic field that studies the problem and its known solutions:

(a) BPM as a problem: People, organizations, and systems run processes in many domains, such as manufacturing, healthcare, or logistics. It is an undeniable fact that in these domains resources are limited. Therefore, managing processes is essential in almost all domains. In other words, the analysis, planning, design, implementation, and monitoring of processes are practical problems in the daily work of many people in almost every organization.

(b) BPM as a solution: In both academia and industry, numerous ideas have emerged to deal with BPM. The proposed solutions include: (a) general frameworks, e.g., the six core framework of [1], (b) lifecycle models, e.g., [2], (c) modeling approaches, e.g., BPMN, (d) specific algorithms, e.g., algorithms for process discovery, or (e) available software tools. Each of these artifacts can be interpreted as a solution to a BPM problem.

(c) BPM as an academic field of research: BPM has a long tradition of research ([3,4,5]). Considering the wide and heterogeneous spectrum of various BPM problems and solutions, it is not surprising that the field is interdisciplinary by nature and is rooted in different academic disciplines. Some important branches of the field and their main outlets for publishing results are: Business Process Management Journal (since 1995), International Conference on Business Process Management (since 2003), or – more specialized – International Conference on Application and Theory of Petri Nets (since 1980), International Conference on Process Mining (since 2019). Furthermore, many major journals or conferences have special BPM sections, e.g. Business and Information Systems Engineering, International and European Conferences on Information Systems, or International Conference on Wirtschaftsinformatik. Last, but not least, the term “ process science ” has recently been used as a name for the field ([6]) and for a newly founded journal.

The problems, solutions, and branches of BPM provide a rich picture of different academic ideas that are important for our discipline. Against this background, the search for the theoretical foundations of process science is of great importance: What are the field’s core concepts? What are the core phenomena? What are the assumptions of the scientific community? Which hypotheses are controversial?

This research explores the theoretical foundations of the field of process science. It proceeds as follows: After this introduction, Section 2 examines the fundamental problem in more detail. A well-accepted scientific background of our study is summarized in Section 3. Section 4, the main part of the paper, proposes a framework as a theoretical foundation of our field by means of an example. The following Sections 5 and 6 discuss related work and conclude our argumentation.
